social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, 20 pack-years, quit 5 years ago

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral foot numbness, tingling, and burning pain for 3 years
patient.history_present_illness: A 62-year-old retired truck driver with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presented to the neurology outpatient clinic reporting progressive bilateral foot numbness, tingling, and burning pain over the past three years. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes approximately 8 years ago and has had persistently poor glycemic control — his last three HbA1c values over the past year were 10.2%, 10.6%, and 10.4%. His primary care physician has adjusted his regimen multiple times without sustained improvement. He describes the foot symptoms as starting with tingling in the tips of his toes bilaterally, which gradually crept up toward his ankles and now extends to mid-calf level. The burning pain is worst at night — it frequently disrupts his sleep, and he describes a sensation like 'standing on hot coals.' He has noticed that his feet feel numb when walking and he has cut himself twice on small objects he did not feel underfoot. He recently knocked over a glass of water that he thought was on his left foot — he did not feel the water at all. He reports no significant weakness, though he has had difficulty with fine foot movements such as picking objects up with his toes. There is no upper extremity involvement. He has not noticed any changes in his handwriting or grip. He denies bowel dysfunction but notes mild constipation occasionally and his wife notices he sweats less than he used to. He has been told his blood sugars are 'way too high' and he has recently started insulin per his internist. He was referred to neurology for formal evaluation of peripheral neuropathy.

neurological_exam.motor: Mild bilateral distal toe extensor weakness (EHL 4/5 bilaterally). Ankle dorsiflexion 4+/5 bilaterally. Proximal strength full. No atrophy of thenar or intrinsic hand muscles.
neurological_exam.sensory: Severe deficit to light touch, pinprick, and temperature in a stocking distribution to mid-calf bilaterally. Vibration severely reduced at great toes and ankles bilaterally. Position sense reduced at great toes. Hands and upper extremities normal.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally. Knee jerks 1+ bilaterally. Upper extremity reflexes 2+ throughout. Plantar flexors bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly ataxic bilaterally (proprioceptive loss).
neurological_exam.gait: Mild sensory ataxia. Steppage gait present bilaterally. Cannot walk on heels. Romberg positive.
neurological_exam.additional: No pes cavus. No hammer toes. Dry skin on bilateral feet. Small healed ulcer scar on right plantar surface.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Glucose 218 mg/dL (H), HbA1c 10.4 % (H), Vitamin B12 198 pg/mL (L), Methylmalonic acid (MMA) 0.34 umol/L (H), Homocysteine 18.4 umol/L (H), ESR 28 mm/hr (H).

findings.pattern: Reduced amplitude, mild DML prolongation — primary axonal
Normal — no upper extremity involvement yet

quantitative_data.distribution: Bilateral lower extremities with stocking distribution

specialized_test.impression: Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, moderate-severe, bilaterally symmetric. NCS shows severely reduced SNAP amplitudes in bilateral sural and peroneal nerves. Motor NCS show reduced CMAP amplitudes with mild DML prolongation (axonal with secondary demyelination at nerve terminals). EMG shows chronic active denervation (fibrillations, PSWs) in distal lower extremity muscles. Upper extremity NCS normal — no length-dependent involvement of arms yet. Pattern is fully consistent with diabetic peripheral polyneuropathy (DPPN). Coexisting B12 deficiency may be contributing to the severity.
recommended_actions: B12 supplementation (oral cyanocobalamin or IM if malabsorption)
Consider switching metformin to alternative agent or reduce dose if glycemic control allows
Neuropathic pain management (gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine)
Foot care and podiatry referral — risk of ulcers given sensory loss

output.test_type: Autonomic testing (QSART, heart rate variability, sudomotor testing)

findings.finding: Reduced sweat output bilateral lower extremities — absent at forefoot bilaterally, reduced at leg and distal forearm. Pattern consistent with length-dependent small fiber autonomic neuropathy.
Reduced HRV on deep breathing — expiration:inspiration ratio 1.08 (normal >1.20). Consistent with cardiac autonomic neuropathy.
Reduced ratio 1.32 (normal >1.5) — consistent with autonomic dysfunction

output.impression: Autonomic neuropathy confirmed — reduced sweating (sudomotor dysfunction), reduced HRV (cardiac autonomic neuropathy). Consistent with diabetic autonomic neuropathy superimposed on sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Increased cardiac risk — refer to cardiology for assessment.
recommended_actions: Cardiology referral for cardiac autonomic neuropathy risk assessment
Foot care — absent sweating increases dry skin/fissure risk

interactions: Metformin — reduces B12 absorption via calcium-dependent ileal membrane mechanism; oral B12 supplementation with calcium salts may partially mitigate this effect
warnings: Monitor B12 levels annually while on metformin
Consider switching from metformin if B12 deficiency worsens and oral supplementation insufficient
Cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily or 1000 mcg IM monthly are equivalent for most patients
alternatives: Methylcobalamin 500-1000 mcg daily — preferred by some neurologists for neuropathy

output.proposed: Gabapentin or duloxetine for diabetic neuropathic pain
interactions: Duloxetine — mild CYP2D6 inhibitor; interaction with no current medications at this dose
Gabapentin — additive CNS sedation with alcohol (patient drinks 2-3 beers daily — counsel on alcohol reduction)
warnings: Patient drinks 2-3 beers daily — gabapentin has additive CNS sedation; counsel on alcohol reduction
Duloxetine is first-line FDA-approved for DPNP and has cardiovascular benefits
Pregabalin is Schedule V controlled — consider this in context of alcohol use
alternatives: Duloxetine 60 mg daily (first-line FDA-approved for DPNP)
Gabapentin 300-600 mg three times daily (monitor sedation given alcohol)

output.test_type: Podiatric examination and diabetic foot risk assessment

findings.finding: Bilateral sensory loss confirmed (monofilament 10g — absent at all plantar sites)
Healing ulcer scar right plantar surface — prior undetected lesion
Dry skin, absent sweating bilateral feet
findings.result: High risk for fissures and infection

output.impression: High-risk diabetic foot — complete sensory loss, prior ulcer, dry skin. Annual podiatry visits minimum; consider more frequent visits. Orthotic insoles, proper footwear, daily foot inspection by patient or caregiver.
recommended_actions: Daily foot inspection — use mirror or have wife assist

output.query: diabetic peripheral neuropathy glycemic control prevention progression

results.title: DCCT/EDIC: intensive glycemic control and diabetic neuropathy risk
results.key_finding: Intensive glycemic control (HbA1c <7%) reduces incident neuropathy by 60% in T1DM; T2DM benefit less dramatic but still significant for preventing progression

results.title: Role of GLP-1 agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetic neuropathy
results.key_finding: SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists may have neuroprotective effects independent of glycemic control — emerging evidence

output.summary: Aggressive glycemic control is the only proven disease-modifying treatment for DPNP. HbA1c 10.4% represents severe undertreatment. Target HbA1c <7% for neuropathy prevention. Consider intensification with insulin, GLP-1 agonist, or SGLT2 inhibitor. Symptomatic treatment with duloxetine (FDA-approved DPNP), gabapentin/pregabalin (counsel on alcohol interaction), or TCA for refractory pain.

output.query: alcohol neuropathy diabetic neuropathy dual etiology

results.title: Alcohol and diabetic neuropathy — synergistic nerve damage
results.key_finding: Alcohol causes independent axonal neuropathy and worsens diabetic neuropathy; 2-3 drinks/day is in the neurotoxic range; cessation is recommended

output.summary: This patient's 2-3 beers/day alcohol consumption likely contributes to his neuropathy beyond diabetes alone. Alcohol causes independent length-dependent axonal neuropathy via nutritional (thiamine, B12) and direct neurotoxic mechanisms. Alcohol cessation is a critical therapeutic recommendation alongside glycemic optimization.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Diabetic peripheral polyneuropathy (DPNP) — length-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy

Metformin-induced B12 deficiency (MMA elevated, B12 198); contributing to severity. Primary diagnosis is DPNP.
No demyelinating features on NCS (no marked velocity slowing, no conduction block, no temporal dispersion). Axonal pattern is fully consistent with DPNP.
No family history, no pes cavus, no hammer toes, adult onset with clear diabetic etiology

critical_actions: HbA1c 10.4% requires urgent glycemic optimization — primary disease-modifying intervention
B12 supplementation mandatory — metformin-induced functional deficiency contributing to neuropathy
Alcohol cessation counseling — 2-3 beers/day is neurotoxic and worsens DPNP
Podiatry referral — high-risk diabetic foot with prior ulcer scar and complete sensory loss

Prescribing pregabalin (Schedule V) or opioids without addressing 2-3 beers/day alcohol use
Diagnosing CIDP or hereditary neuropathy without supporting features — NCS pattern is clearly axonal DPNP
key_reasoning_points: Classic DPNP: length-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy in a patient with very poorly controlled T2DM (HbA1c 10.4%)
Metformin-induced B12 deficiency (MMA elevated) is a contributing factor — B12 supplementation required
Alcohol 2-3 beers/day provides an independent neurotoxic contribution — cessation counseling essential

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: B12 deficiency is a contributing factor (metformin-related) but the primary diagnosis is DPNP from HbA1c 10.4%. Both require treatment.
